steps.say: Seven calls to nasm, one call to ld, and no compiler anywhere.
What comes out is a static binary with no dynamic section. Then it answers a question, as Qwen3-0.6B.
steps.caption: 12,120 bytes, no dynamic section

scenes.headline: llm.asm: a language model in 12 KB of assembly
scenes.sub: The kernel, the threads, the polynomials, and a 24 KB OS
scenes.say: I'm Mnemonic. Let's open the binary and see what does the work.

heads: Quantize the activations once per matmul
Move the sign onto the weights

rows.w: weights: int8, scale beside the row

steps.say: Before any thread wakes, the activation vector becomes int8, with one scale per block of thirty-two.
steps.term: Q8_0: 32 int8 weights sharing one scale

steps.say: The multiply instruction wants one unsigned side. So take the absolute value of x, and push its sign onto the weights.
Thirty-two byte products, folded pairwise into sixteen lanes. Both sides are clamped, so the sums never overflow.
Multiply by ones to fold again, into eight exact integers.
Convert to float, multiply by the two block scales, and add into one of four accumulators.

left.title: llama.cpp
left.say: llama.cpp uses the same sign trick and the same two instructions, one block at a time into a single accumulator.

right.title: llm.asm
right.say: llm.asm unrolls four blocks into four accumulators, over rows that start on a cache line.

scenes.title: Four threads, my i7-14700
scenes.note: A shared machine; read the ratio
scenes.say: I ran it myself on a busy desktop chip. At four threads the integer kernel decoded about one and a half times faster than llama.cpp.

stations.label: clone
stations.sub: a stack, shared memory, no return

steps.say: A thread is a raw clone call with its own stack.
Workers spin on a counter, so a new job costs no syscall.
Only when the user goes quiet do they sleep on a futex.
Each one reports done on its own cache line, so no counter bounces between cores.
Every row belongs to one thread, so the output is identical at any thread count.
steps.term: Static partition: same row, same thread, same bits

steps.say: But nobody yields. On my shared machine, with more threads than free cores, every barrier waited on a descheduled worker, and decode collapsed.
Both engines climb, then flatten past sixteen threads.
That plateau is memory. At its peak, llm.asm streams about eighty gigabytes a second of weights.
Then the second post deleted Linux. A diskless VM, two gigabytes, every core near a hundred percent.
It boots straight into a chat. With no scheduler, a core spins or it works.
steps.caption: Xeon E5-2670 v3, 12 cores, no disk

steps.say: The kernel maps the first four gigabytes in two-megabyte pages and finds the weights at a physical address.
It wakes every core over the APIC and prints its own timings.

scenes.title: Splitting the 54%
scenes.say: Most of the headline runs on Linux already. The OS adds the last slice, and huge pages on Linux should win most of that back.

left.title: Hugging Face
left.say: Hugging Face splits the text with a regex first, and the last space stays with the word.

right.title: llm.asm
right.say: The assembly skips that split. On my run, five of twelve strings came out different, every one a run of whitespace.

scenes.text: Steal the layout. The assembly is the demo.
scenes.say: Split rows, fused projections, four accumulators, one owner per row. None of it needs assembly.

recap: The OS adds the last slice
scenes.say: llm.asm: twelve kilobytes that read six hundred megabytes, every token.
